page1.subtitle: Evidence key: observed = a measured signal or sample; inferred = an explanation/model; unknown ≠ absent. Habitable ≠ inhabited. No confirmed extraterrestrial life.
worlds: Venus

Rocky planet, second from Sun (≈0.72 AU). CO<sub>2</sub>-rich air, sulfuric-acid clouds; surface ≈467°C, ≈93 Earth atmospheres. High albedo reflects sunlight, yet strong infrared greenhouse warming dominates surface temperature.

Surface hostile to known life. Milder cloud temperatures do not remove extreme acidity and very low water availability. Ancient ocean history is unresolved; phosphine claims are disputed, not life evidence. Venus Express / DAVINCI / VERITAS.
Mars

Rocky planet, fourth from Sun (≈1.52 AU). Thin CO<sub>2</sub> air (≈6 mbar), cold dry surface, water ice. Valleys, deltas, lake sediments and hydrated minerals record past liquid water. Solar-driven escape helped alter the atmosphere.

Past habitable settings ≠ past life. Exposed liquid is difficult to sustain now. Organics and potential biosignatures require abiotic tests and context; radiation/oxidants damage preservation. Perseverance = local rocks; MRO = regional record; MAVEN = escape.
Ganymede

Diameter ≈5,260 km. Jupiter’s moon; largest moon in the Solar System. Intrinsic magnetic field is distinct from an induced ocean response. Magnetic/auroral behavior supports a conducting salty interior layer; icy, grooved and cratered terrain.

Likely deep ocean with complex water/ice layers. High-pressure ice may restrict rock contact; exchange, nutrients and energy remain uncertain. Tenuous O<sub>2</sub> is not breathable air or life evidence. Galileo / JUICE.
Europa

Diameter ≈3,120 km. Jupiter’s moon. Fractured young ice and induced magnetic response strongly support a salty ocean over rock. Surface CO<sub>2</sub> concentrated in young terrain favors an internal carbon source.

Tidal heat; possible water-rock chemistry and surface oxidant delivery. Radiation damages exposed organics. Exchange and plume activity uncertain. Ice thickness is regional/model-dependent, not one exact global value. Galileo / Europa Clipper.
Enceladus

Diameter ≈500 km. Saturn’s moon. South-polar fractures eject water-rich gas and icy grains. Cassini sampled salts, organics and H<sub>2</sub>; phosphate found in grains. Evidence strongly supports an internal ocean.

H<sub>2</sub> supports rock-water reactions and possible usable chemical energy, not microbes. Plumes provide access without drilling but may filter/alter ocean material. Ocean longevity, concentrations and life remain unknown. Cassini.
Titan

Diameter ≈5,150 km. Saturn’s largest moon; second-largest moon in the Solar System. Surface pressure ≈1.5 Earth sea-level; dense N<sub>2</sub> air, methane haze/weather; methane/ethane lakes and rivers over a water-ice surface (≈94 K). Rich organic chemistry. Water is not the liquid in the surface lakes.

Known life uses water, not liquid methane. Impact melt could mix water and organics. A 2025 Cassini reanalysis favors slushy high-pressure ice over a global ocean in tested models; melt pockets possible, not observed habitats. Cassini-Huygens / Dragonfly.
Makemake

Diameter ≈1,430 km; orbits Sun beyond Neptune. Cold Kuiper Belt dwarf planet (≈46 AU). Spectra show methane/ethane ice; reported methane gas has competing bound-atmosphere and escaping-gas interpretations.

No established ocean or stable surface-water habitat. Isotopes constrain methane origins but permit competing internal/primordial models. Very low solar flux; internal structure poorly known. Methane alone is not biological.
Near-Earth, carbon-rich rubble-pile asteroid ≈500 m across. Returned samples contain hydrated minerals, salts, amino acids, nucleobases and sugars. Ancient parent-body alteration/brines inferred.

Ingredients and chemical history, not cells, DNA or a present Bennu ocean. Small bodies can deliver water-bearing material/organics; delivery does not explain all steps to life. Contamination-controlled laboratories distinguish native material. OSIRIS-REx.

67P/
Churyumov-
Gerasimenko

Jupiter-family comet; orbits Sun, not Jupiter, about every 6.5 yr. Comet nucleus releases ice as vapor and dust under solar heating; coma/jets ≠ stable dense atmosphere. Rosetta found water, organics including glycine, phosphorus and molecular oxygen.

Mostly ice/vapor does not imply a liquid-water habitat. O<sub>2</sub> and organics can be abiotic. Water D/H is an origin tracer, with sampling/model disputes; one comet cannot establish all of Earth’s water sources. Rosetta / Philae.
systems: Seven roughly Earth-size transiting planets b-h around an ultracool M dwarf. e/f/g lie in commonly modeled surface-water habitable zones; short orbits aid repeated observations.

Stellar flares/heterogeneity affect planets and spectra. b/c thick atmospheres disfavored; do not extrapolate to all planets. Tested extended H<sub>2</sub>/He air on f disfavored; heavier air unresolved. Atmospheres, water and life are not established by HZ position.
G-type host; transiting b has radius ≈1.6 Earth radii, period ≈385 d, orbit ≈1.05 AU. An older/more luminous star changes received flux despite an Earth-like orbital distance.

Detection reliability is controversial in the NASA Exoplanet Archive. Transit constrains radius ratio/period, not surface, ocean or directly measured mass. Atmosphere, water and surface temperature remain unknown.
M dwarf; b transits every ≈24.7 d, ≈1.73 Earth radii and ≈5.6 Earth masses in recent analyses. Interior/spectral models allow a water-rich interpretation.

Water world and nitrogen-rich air are hypotheses, not detections. A 2026 helium claim from one ground-based transit is disputed by analyses of four non-simultaneous JWST transits; variability vs false signal unresolved. Non-detection ≠ no atmosphere.
page1.end: One AU ≈150 million km (Earth–Sun orbital scale); moon–planet distance is a different scale. Compare, do not rank by slogans: solvent phase + pressure/temperature + usable energy + accessible chemistry + transport + persistence. Interior drawings are models. A spectrum, rock texture or molecule is a clue whose alternatives must be tested. Secondary atmosphere: replenished (e.g., outgassing), not simply primordial gas; not necessarily Earth-like.

page2.subtitle: Ask where, when, in what phase, with what energy, and for how long? Distinguish a heat source that maintains liquid from a chemical reaction that could power metabolism.

columns.title: 1. Requirements and useful distinctions
items: Known Earth life: liquid water, carbon-based chemistry, accessible elements/nutrients (including C, H, N, O, P, S), usable energy and conditions that allow chemistry and persistence. One favorable ingredient is insufficient.

Habitable = potentially capable of supporting life under specified conditions; inhabited = life actually present. Organic compounds are carbon-based, often with C-H bonds, not necessarily biological; not all carbon compounds are organic (CO2 is inorganic). Prebiotic = relevant to processes before life.

Surface-water habitable zone (HZ): stellar-distance range in which suitable atmospheres could sustain surface liquid water. Depends on star/air/models; excludes neither buried oceans outside it nor hostile planets inside it.

columns.title: 2. Energy budget, atmosphere and retention
items: Flux decreases as 1/d². Albedo reflects a fraction of incident light. Greenhouse effect: air absorbs/emits infrared; the surface must warm to balance energy loss to space. High reflectivity and a strong greenhouse can coexist (Venus).

Equilibrium temperature is an idealized radiative balance, not automatically surface temperature. Greenhouse, day/night transport, clouds, internal heat and emissivity matter. Use Kelvin in thermal laws.

Retention: greater mass/smaller radius raises escape speed; hotter and lighter particles move faster. Thermal escape preferentially removes fast particles. UV heating/ionization, stellar winds and nonthermal processes can increase loss. Volcanism/delivery can replenish air.

Do not use one cause: atmosphere depends on gravity, temperature, chemistry, star, history and replenishment. No intrinsic magnetic field does not imply no atmosphere; Venus is a counterexample. Loss rates vary with time.

columns.title: 3. Water forms are not interchangeable
items: Liquid: mobile solvent; stable only within a pressure-temperature-composition range. Crystalline ice: ordered lattice; different high-pressure phases exist. Amorphous ice: disordered solid, able to trap volatiles; not liquid.

Brine: salts dissolved in water can depress freezing temperature; highly saline water can have too little water activity for known life. Clathrate: water-ice cages enclose guest gas molecules; not a liquid solution.

Pure-water phase map: triple point ≈273.16 K and 611 Pa; below that pressure ordinary stable liquid cannot persist. Low-pressure warming often gives sublimation (solid→gas), not melting. Pressure/brines change stability.

Water evidence: vapor, surface frost, bound water in minerals, ancient lake deposits and inferred current ocean mean different things. Hydrated minerals record alteration; they do not alone prove liquid exists now.

columns.title: 4. Internal energy and transport
items: Heat sources: radioactive decay, retained formation heat and tidal dissipation. Tidal gravity is a differential force; time-varying deformation plus dissipation creates heat. Resonances can maintain orbital eccentricity and flexing.

Cryovolcanism: eruption/transport of volatile-rich liquids, slurries or gases instead of silicate lava. Fractures or plumes may exchange interior/surface material, but a landform alone does not fix composition or source depth.

Why rock contact matters: water-rock reactions may supply H2, dissolved nutrients and redox gradients. High-pressure ice can impede exchange; circulation and mixing determine access. Heat alone is not food.

columns.title: 5. Chemistry that can power life
items: Equilibrium: forward/reverse rates balance; concentrations stay constant, not necessarily equal. Disequilibrium: composition differs from equilibrium; a usable chemical gradient can release free energy as it relaxes.
Redox: electrons transfer from donors to acceptors. Energy-yielding chemistry needs both, adequate concentrations and mixing. Sunlight or geological reactions can replenish disequilibrium.
Chemolithoautotroph: chemical energy (chemo), inorganic electron donors (litho), inorganic carbon/CO2 for biomass (auto). Needs a compatible reaction; sunlight is not its immediate energy source.
Earth metabolic analogy: CO2 + 4H2 → CH4 + 2H2O. Some microbes use this chemistry; abiotic reactions can also make methane. H2 at Enceladus supports energy potential, not methanogen detection.

columns.title: 6. Building blocks and extremophiles
items: Proteins: amino-acid polymers; enzymes catalyze and structures perform work. Nucleic acids: nucleotide polymers DNA/RNA store/transmit information; a nucleotide includes base, sugar and phosphate.

Lipids: many membrane lipids are amphiphilic and form compartments; other lipids store energy. Carbohydrates: sugars/polymers used in energy and structure. Amino acids, bases or sugars ≠ functioning cells or their polymers.
Extremophiles: organisms adapted to extremes; thermophiles (heat), psychrophiles (cold), halophiles (salt), acidophiles (acid). Limits interact; tolerance to one does not imply tolerance to all.
Tardigrades: some survive dehydration/extreme exposures while dormant. Survival ≠ metabolism/reproduction there. Duration, protective state and species matter; not proof life grows in vacuum.

columns.title: 7. Read morphology, spectra and samples
items: Valleys/channels: geometry, branching, slope and deposits test flowing-liquid interpretations. Deltas: deposited sediment at a flow entering a standing body. Layers: changing deposition; not every layer is a lake.
Context test: distinguish water erosion from wind, lava, ice or impacts. Grain rounding/sorting and clay/sulfate minerals constrain processes; a familiar-looking shape is not decisive.

Spectrum: brightness/reflectance vs wavelength. Repeated absorption/emission bands support material identification; band depths depend on abundance, grain size, temperature, mixing, clouds and geometry. Compare a baseline and uncertainty.

Small-body delivery: impacts can deliver organics/water-bearing material; later heating/chemistry alters it. Isotope ratios (e.g., D/H) trace sources but mixtures and processing complicate attribution. Ingredients ≠ organisms.

columns.title: 8. Evidence ladder and answer checklist
items: Observation → inference → alternative → test. Example: a spectral band → candidate molecule → overlapping species/instrument effect → multiple bands and independent calibration. Name what the instrument actually measured.

Biosignature: a feature potentially produced by life, evaluated against abiotic sources, contamination and preservation. Multiple independent contextual clues are stronger than one gas. O2, CH4 and organics can be abiotic.

Non-detection: applies to a place, epoch, sample and sensitivity; not universal absence. Cloudy/heavy atmospheres can hide bands. Sampling, detection limits, error bars and model assumptions belong in the conclusion.
Maps/plots: check scale, units, orientation, axes, legend, baseline and error bars. Correlation ≠ cause; a fitting model need not be unique. Separate direct, historical and model-derived claims.

page3.subtitle: Status key: C completed/retired; A active operations; cruise not yet at target science; P planned. Instruments below are key examples, not exhaustive payload lists.

missions.name: Venus Express
missions.text: Atmosphere/climate/escape: VIRTIS + SPICAV/SOIR spectra; VMC clouds; ASPERA-4 particles; MAG fields; VeRa radio profiles. Repeated global views avoid surface heat/pressure, but do not directly sample the deep atmosphere.

missions.name: DAVINCI
missions.text: Atmospheric history: VMS noble/trace gases/isotopes; VTLS chemistry; VASI pressure/T/winds; VenDI descent images; VfOx oxygen chemistry. VISOR/CUVIS on carrier. One protected descent profile depends on a short relay window, not long surface survival.

missions.name: VERITAS
missions.text: Geologic evolution/activity: VISAR radar images, topography and deformation; VEM near-IR emissivity; radio gravity. Radar sees through clouds; composition/interior remain indirect. Repeat geometry, data volume and thermal control constrain mapping.

missions.name: Perseverance
missions.text: Ancient habitability/potential biosignatures: Mastcam-Z context; SuperCam remote chemistry; PIXL elements; SHERLOC minerals/organics; RIMFAX layers; MEDA weather; cores cached. MMRTG + mobility, but local coverage/contamination limits. MOXIE O<sub>2</sub> demo ended.

missions.name: MRO
missions.text: HiRISE detail + CTX context; CRISM mineral spectra (retired instrument, useful archive); SHARAD subsurface radar; MARCI/MCS weather/air profiles. Regional mapping + rover relay. Resolution trades against footprint/data; radar echoes need interpretation.

missions.name: MAVEN
missions.text: Escape and atmosphere evolution: NGIMS composition/isotopes; IUVS UV structure; SWIA/SWEA/SEP/STATIC particles; MAG/LPW fields/plasma. Elliptical orbit connects air and space. Present loss rates cannot simply be extrapolated over billions of years.

missions.name: Galileo
missions.text: Moon geology/ocean clues: camera, NIMS spectra, magnetic/plasma data; separate probe sampled Jupiter’s air. RTGs and shielding enabled distant science; failed high-gain antenna restricted data. Controlled Jupiter entry reduced moon-contamination risk.

missions.name: Europa Clipper
missions.text: Europa habitability: EIS images, MISE chemistry, E-THEMIS heat, UVS atmosphere, REASON ice radar; ECM+PIMS ocean/plasma; MASPEX gas, SUDA dust; radio gravity. Brief flybys reduce radiation dose; large solar arrays. Not a lander or life detector.

missions.name: JUICE
missions.text: Compare icy moons: JANUS images; MAJIS/UVS/SWI spectra; GALA topography; RIME ice radar; J-MAG fields, PEP/RPWI plasma, 3GM gravity/radio. Solar wings/shielding; eventual Ganymede orbit gives sustained coverage versus short flybys elsewhere.

missions.name: Cassini-Huygens
missions.text: Cassini RADAR mapped Titan; INMS gas + CDA grains sampled Enceladus; cameras/spectrometers/fields supplied context. Huygens GCMS chemistry, DISR images, HASI atmosphere, DWE winds, SSP surface. RTG orbiter vs short battery/relay descent.

missions.name: Dragonfly
missions.text: Prebiotic chemistry: DrACO samples → DraMS compounds; DraGNS elements; DragonCam context; DraGMet weather/geophysics. Dense air/low gravity favor flight between sites. MMRTG charges flight battery; autonomy needed, sunlight weak.

missions.name: OSIRIS-REx
missions.text: OCAMS images; OLA shape; OVIRS/OTES spectra; TAGSAM collected material for Earth laboratories. Precise low-gravity navigation, safe return and contamination control trade complexity for powerful repeatable analyses. Samples remain under study; spacecraft continued renamed.

missions.name: Rosetta
missions.text: OSIRIS images; ROSINA gases/isotopes; COSIMA dust chemistry; VIRTIS/ALICE/MIRO spectra; CONSERT interior radio. Followed changing comet activity. Dust/low gravity challenge navigation; Philae bounced into shade, limiting solar recharge.

missions.name: Kepler
missions.text: CCD photometer tracked many stars’ brightness to infer planet periods/radius ratios and occurrence. Stable pointing/long baseline detect tiny repeating dips; only aligned systems transit. Correct census for geometric and detection bias; no planet surface pictures.

missions.name: JWST
missions.text: NIRCam, NIRSpec, NIRISS and MIRI: imaging/spectra; transits, eclipses/phase curves and selected direct imaging constrain gases/heat. Sunshield + MIRI cryocooler reduce thermal noise. Stellar contamination/clouds and retrieval degeneracy limit claims.

missions.name: Roman Space Telescope
missions.text: WFI will survey bulge microlensing/transits; Coronagraph tests starlight suppression. NASA reports instrument alignment complete, further coronagraph tests ahead. Many stars catch rare events; cadence and distant targets limit follow-up.

columns.title: Transits and radial velocity (RV)
items: Transit: relative stellar flux vs time; δ=(Fout−Fin)/Fout≈(Rp/R★)²; repeated centers → P. Nearly edge-on; favors large, close-in planets/small stars. Blends, binaries, starspots can mislead. Gives radius, not mass; duration ≠ period.

RV: periodic stellar spectral-line shifts → line-of-sight velocity. K is half peak-to-peak amplitude; orbit + stellar mass → Mp sin i (minimum mass). i=90° edge-on; face-on gives no RV wobble. Favors massive/short-period planets; stellar activity mimics signals.
Combine: transit radius + RV mass → mean density; ρ∝M/R³. Density still permits different interiors. Atmospheric spectra can add chemistry, not automatic habitability.

columns.title: What an instrument really measures
items: Imager: brightness/position → morphology. Light spectrometer: intensity/wavelength → composition/T. Mass spectrometer: ion mass/charge → sampled chemistry. Radar: echo delay/strength → interfaces. Magnetometer: field → conductivity models. Radio tracking: motion → gravity/interior. No one instrument is a universal “life scanner.”

columns.title: Microlensing and direct imaging
items: Microlensing: foreground gravity magnifies a background star; a planetary perturbation changes flux vs time. Model yields mass ratio/projected separation in lens units; extra constraints needed for absolute mass. Sensitive to cold/wide and unbound planets; rare alignment, usually nonrepeating. Duration mixes mass, distance and relative speed.

Direct imaging: suppress stellar glare with a coronagraph, separate planet light → brightness/colors/spectra and position. Favors wide, nearby, young/hot giant planets. Contrast, diffraction and inner working angle hide close faint planets. Brightness-to-mass conversion depends on age/atmosphere models; unresolved dot ≠ surface map.

columns.title: Choose the platform; pay the tradeoff
items: Orbiter: repeated/global but indirect. Flyby: low close-range exposure, short window. Probe/rover: direct local data, landing risk/limited area. Return: best labs, costly collection/reentry/cleanliness.

Power: solar ∝1/d²; RTGs convert radioactive heat, not fission. Batteries store energy. Comms: distance lowers signal, increases delay; antennas/relays/autonomy help. Shielding, thermal control and clean handling cost mass/power. Protect samples and potentially habitable worlds.

page4.subtitle: Use ratios before arithmetic; name assumptions; cancel units; keep Kelvin and consistent distances. Symbols are defined in each box. Subscripts distinguish star (★), planet (p), and reference values (0).

columns.title: 1. Doppler shift and transit size
columns.formula:
vr/c ≈ Δλ/λ0; Δλ = λobs − λ0
δ ≈ (Rp/R★)²; Rp ≈ R★√δ
items: v<sub>r</sub>: signed radial velocity; c: light speed; λ: wavelength (same units). Valid |v|≪c. Positive shift = recession; negative = approach. At 500 nm, +0.00005 nm → +30 m/s.
δ: fractional flux decrease; 1%=0.01 → radius ratio 0.1. Depth ×4 → radius ×2. Uniform unblended star, dark non-grazing planet; real fits include limb darkening. P=spacing of successive centers.

columns.title: 2. Flux, albedo and inverse-square law
items: L luminosity [W]; F incident flux [W/m²]; d star-planet distance [m]; R<sub>p</sub> radius. Bond albedo A is the fraction of total incident power reflected (0-1). Absorbed fraction is 1−A, not A.
d ×2 → F ÷4; L ×4 → F ×4 at fixed d. Spreading area=4πd²; planet intercepts πR<sub>p</sub>². F vs d falls/curves; log F vs log d slope −2 at fixed L.

columns.title: 3. Thermal emission and wavelength
items: T in K; ε emissivity (0-1); σ Stefan-Boltzmann constant; b Wien constant. Emitted flux is power/area, luminosity is total power. ε=1 gives an ideal blackbody.
T ×2 → flux ×16 and peak wavelength ÷2. At fixed T, R ×2 → luminosity ×4, not surface flux ×4. Wien is a wavelength-spectrum peak; hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths.

columns.title: 4. Equilibrium temperature
items: Assumes steady balance, uniform reradiation over full sphere, no internal heat; greenhouse not included. R<sub>p</sub> cancels. With ε=1: T<sub>eq</sub>=T<sub>★</sub>√[R<sub>★</sub>/(2d)](1−A)<super>1/4</super>.

T<sub>eq</sub>∝L<super>1/4</super>d<super>−1/2</super>(1−A)<super>1/4</super>. L ×16 → T ×2; d ×4 → T ÷2; absorbed fraction ×16 → T ×2. Not linear in flux or necessarily surface T. Redistribution changes the factor 4.

columns.title: 5. Ideal gas and particle motion
items: P pressure [Pa]; V volume [m³]; n amount [mol]; N molecule count; R<sub>g</sub> molar gas constant; k<sub>B</sub> per-particle constant. Use a dilute ideal-gas approximation, not arbitrary dense fluids.
Fixed n,V: P∝T; fixed n,T: P∝1/V; fixed n,P: V∝T. 300→600 K doubles P at fixed V, not 30→60°C. T ×4 → thermal speed ×2; particle mass ×4 → speed ÷2.

columns.title: 6. Chemical equilibrium and kinetics
columns.formula:
aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD; Keq = aCcaDd/(aAaaBb)
k = Apreexp[−Ea/(RgT)]
ln k = ln Apre − (Ea/Rg)(1/T)
items: a<sub>i</sub>: dimensionless activity; coefficients become powers. Dilute models may use normalized concentrations; pure solids/liquids omitted. Q has the same form at current composition: Q<K forward favored; Q>K reverse.

Arrhenius: k rate constant, A<sub>pre</sub> prefactor, E<sub>a</sub> activation energy [J/mol]. For positive E<sub>a</sub>, warmer → faster. ln k vs 1/T has slope −E<sub>a</sub>/R<sub>g</sub>. Catalyst lowers barrier/speeds approach, not K or equilibrium composition. Rate ≠ equilibrium; balance atoms first.

columns.title: 7. Gravity, energy and escape
columns.formula:
Fg = GMm/r²; g = GM/r²
EK = ½mv²; U = −GMm/r (U∞=0)
vesc = √(2GM/R); vcirc = √(GM/r)
items: G gravitational constant; M central mass, m test mass [kg]; r center-to-center separation, R launch radius [m]. Force [N]; acceleration [m/s²]; energy [J]. Use radius, not diameter or height above surface alone.

Minimum escape speed: ½mv²−GMm/R=0 for arrival at infinity with zero speed (neglect drag/rotation). m cancels; v<sub>esc</sub>=√2 v<sub>circ</sub> at same radius. Escape ≠ orbiting or leaving the atmosphere.
M ×4 → v<sub>esc</sub> ×2 at fixed R. R ×4 → v<sub>esc</sub> ÷2 at fixed M. r ×2 → force/g ÷4. Potential becomes less negative with increasing r; energy must be added to escape.

columns.title: 8. Kepler’s three laws and ellipse geometry
items: 1: elliptical orbit, central object at a focus (two-body model). a=semimajor axis; e=eccentricity (circle e=0; bound ellipse 0≤e<1). a need not equal current r.
2: equal swept areas in equal times → faster near periapsis, slower near apoapsis. 3: at same central mass, P²∝a³. a ×4 → P ×8; central mass ×4 → P ÷2 at same a.

In yr, AU and solar masses: P²≈a³/M<sub>★</sub> when planet mass negligible. P²=a³ alone assumes a solar-mass star. General SI form gives seconds; do not mix units or assume all stars have Sun’s mass.

columns.title: 9. Tides: gradient, not just attraction
items: Approximate near-side-minus-center radial acceleration. Near-to-far difference is about twice this. d center-to-center separation; R<sub>body</sub> satellite radius. At fixed masses/radius: d ×2 → differential acceleration ÷8, not ÷4.

Steady distortion alone is not continuous heating. Changing tides (e.g., eccentric orbit) + material friction/dissipation convert orbital/mechanical energy into heat. Resonances can sustain eccentricity. Heating needs rigidity, viscosity, orbit and dissipation: 1/d³ is not a complete heat-power law.

columns.title: 10. Density, angles and minimum mass
items: M ×8 and R ×2 → same mean density. Density does not uniquely identify composition. 10 AU projected separation at 20 pc → 0.5 arcsec; projected separation need not equal semimajor axis.
RV: i=90° edge-on (sin i=1), i=0° face-on. Minimum mass 4 Earth masses at i=30° → true mass 8. K semi-amplitude is half peak-to-peak range. Transits constrain near-edge-on inclination.

Diffraction scale θ≈1.22λ/D<sub>ap</sub> [radians] for circular aperture; aperture D<sub>ap</sub> ×2 → angular scale ÷2. This is not sufficient by itself: contrast/inner working angle also limit imaging.

columns.title: Units, constants and calculator-free habits
items: Units: 1 Pa=1 N/m²; 1 N=1 kg·m/s²; 1 J=1 N·m; 1 W=1 J/s. 1 nm=10−9 m; 1 km=10³ m; 1 d=86,400 s. T[K]=T[°C]+273.15.
Useful rounded constants: c≈3×10⁸ m/s; G≈6.67×10−11 m³ kg−1 s−2; σ≈5.67×10−8 W m−2 K−4; b≈2.90×10−3 m·K; Rg≈8.31 J mol−1 K−1; kB≈1.38×10−23 J/K; 1 AU≈1.50×1011 m; 1 pc≈3.09×1016 m.

Routine: knowns/unknowns → model → rearrange → ratios/powers of ten → units → physical check. √4=2; √9=3; fourth root 16=2; 1%=10−2. x² rises/curves; 1/x² falls/curves; log y vs log x slope equals power.
Traps: °C in T⁴; % vs fraction; radius vs diameter; center-distance vs altitude; flux vs luminosity; surface vs equilibrium T; K vs 2K; unjustified precision.
